why_two_percent:
Thank you for the question.

We used the 2% importance threshold as a practical rule for removing features with relatively small measured contributions. We wanted a smaller model, but we did not want to prune so aggressively that potentially useful weather information disappeared.

The important point is that 2% was a fixed comparison rule, not a mathematically optimized value. We applied the same cutoff to the LIME-guided Path A and the XGBoost-gain-guided Path B so the two selection methods faced the same numerical rule. That makes the comparison easier to interpret, although their importance percentages are based on different measures.

A different cutoff could retain a different number of features. In fact, the wind-direction feature ddd_x was close to the boundary and crossed it in some LIME seed runs. So I would not claim 2% is universally optimal. Our supported conclusion is narrower: under this stated rule, LIME-guided refinement reduced the feature set while maintaining comparable predictive performance.
contribution:
Thank you for the question. The baseline was already reasonably strong, so our purpose was broader than increasing one test score. We wanted to see whether an explanation method could help us understand and simplify the model, and then compare that workflow fairly with XGBoost's built-in gain importance.

The ablation result is important here. Cyclic encoding alone reached the same hold-out F1 as the full Path A, so we should not say that LIME caused the observed F1 increase. LIME's supported role was diagnostic: it highlighted influential weather features and helped guide a more compact feature set. In the pruning-only experiment, the model went from 22 predictors to 9 while keeping the baseline F1 on the hold-out.

We also checked explanation stability and tested the differences between models. Neither refinement path showed a statistically established predictive advantage. So the main contribution is a careful example of using explainability as feedback for model refinement and interpretation, while being honest about what did and did not improve.
single_station:
Thank you for the question. At this stage, we cannot say that the model would perform equally well in other cities. All observations used in this study came from the Bandung Geophysical Station, WMO 96783, so the fitted model and its feature ranking reflect that station's data.

Another location may have different relationships among humidity, temperature, wind, season, and rainfall. A model trained only on Bandung observations could therefore lose accuracy when moved elsewhere. We did not run that external test in this paper, so any claim of equal performance would go beyond the evidence.

A useful next experiment would be to test the existing model on another station without retraining it. That would show how much transfers directly. We could then retrain or adapt the model with data from that location and compare the result. For now, our performance claim belongs to the Bandung dataset; the LIME-guided refinement procedure itself could be studied elsewhere, but its success there still needs to be demonstrated.
